title: Episode 93: The Amistad Rebellion at New Haven: John Quincy Adams and the Battle for Liberty

In 1839, Sengbe Pieh led an armed mutiny aboard the Spanish slave schooner La Amistad. Brought into New Haven harbor, the captive Africans sparked a monumental legal battle that reached the Supreme Court, championed by former President John Quincy Adams.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we visit the maritime shores and federal courtrooms of New Haven, Connecticut, to witness one of the most consequential legal crusades in American history: the Amistad Rebellion of eighteen thirty-nine. Kidnapped from Sierra Leone in direct violation of international treaties banning the transatlantic slave trade, fifty-three Mende captives broke their iron shackles off the coast of Cuba, seized the schooner La Amistad, and attempted to navigate back to Africa. Intercepted off Long Island and brought to Connecticut, their plight ignited an international diplomatic firestorm that pitted abolitionists against President Martin Van Buren, culminating in a historic legal defense before the United States Supreme Court delivered by former President John Quincy Adams. Here is George with the full, gripping story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: KIDNAPPED ACROSS THE ATLANTIC
In the spring of eighteen thirty-nine, twenty-five-year-old Sengbe Pieh—a proud Mende rice farmer and father of three known later to Americans as Joseph Cinqué—was walking along a peaceful foot trail near his village in modern-day Sierra Leone. Suddenly, four armed men ambushed him from the bush, overpowering him in front of his home and binding his limbs with raw rawhide. Sengbe was sold to local slave brokers and marched through the jungle to the notorious barracoons of Lomboko, an island fortress on the Gallinas coast operated by the infamous Spanish slave trader Pedro Blanco.
At Lomboko, Sengbe was branded like cattle on the right breast and forced into the sweltering, airless hold of the Portuguese slave ship Teçora alongside five hundred other kidnapped Africans. For over two brutal months, the Teçora traversed the Middle Passage across the Atlantic to Havana, Cuba. Nearly a third of the human cargo perished from disease, dehydration, and dysentery, their bodies tossed unceremoniously to the sharks. This human trafficking was completely illegal: both Spain and Great Britain had signed international treaties in eighteen seventeen and eighteen twenty explicitly abolishing the transatlantic slave trade, rendering every African imported into Spanish dominions legally free citizens by natural right.
Yet in the corrupt colonial slave markets of Havana, fraudulent papers were routinely forged with the connivance of the Spanish Captain General. Sengbe and forty-eight adult men and four children were purchased by two wealthy Spanish planters, Pedro Montes and José Ruiz, who obtained falsified passports falsely identifying the newly arrived Mende captives as 'Ladinos'—Spanish-born enslaved persons who had lived in Cuba for years. Under cover of darkness on June twenty-eighth, eighteen thirty-nine, the captives were loaded aboard the coastal schooner La Amistad, bound for plantations in Puerto Príncipe.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: MUTINY IN THE MIDNIGHT TEMPEST
Aboard the two-masted black schooner La Amistad, conditions were intolerable. Packed in chains in the shallow cargo hold with ceiling clearances of less than four feet, the Mende prisoners suffered agonizing thirst under the Caribbean sun. When Sengbe managed to ask the ship's cook, a mulatto named Celestino, what would happen to them when they reached their destination, the cruel cook laughed maliciously, pointing to a large iron butchering cauldron on the deck and gesturing with a carving knife that they would be slaughtered, salted, and eaten by the white planters.
Terrified and determined to die fighting rather than submit to slaughter, Sengbe used a loose piece of rusty iron hoop he discovered hidden in the ballast stones to patiently pick the padlock of his iron neck collar. In the early morning hours of July second, eighteen thirty-nine, as a torrential tropical gale battered the schooner off the northern coast of Cuba, Sengbe freed himself and his fellow Mende warriors. Armed with heavy sugar-cane machetes found in cargo crates in the hold, the men surged onto the rain-swept deck.
In the violent melee that followed, the ship's captain, Ramón Ferrer, fought back with a cutlass, killing two Mende warriors before Sengbe struck him down with a machete. The sadistic cook Celestino was killed, while two crewmen panicked and leaped overboard into a small launch, vanishing into the storm. The two Spanish planters, Ruiz and Montes, surrendered and begged for their lives. Sengbe spared them on one absolute condition: they must take the helm and sail the Amistad directly eastward toward the rising sun, back to the coast of Africa.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE DECEITFUL NAVIGATION AND CAPTURE OFF LONG ISLAND
For nearly two months, the battered schooner wandered in a bizarre and desperate maritime dance across the Atlantic. During the daylight hours, with Sengbe standing watchful guard with a drawn cutlass, the Spanish planters obeyed orders, steering the vessel due east into the rising sun. But when night fell and the stars were obscured by clouds, Pedro Montes, an experienced navigator, subtly altered the ship's course to the north and northwest, hoping to reach the coast of the American South or encounter an American naval vessel.
Instead of reaching the warm shores of Sierra Leone, the Amistad zigzagged thousands of miles up the eastern seaboard of North America. Food and fresh water ran perilously low. Ten Mende captives died of dehydration and fever, and the survivors were reduced to boiling sea biscuits in saltwater. By late August, the ragged, barnacle-encrusted schooner with tattered black sails drifted off Montauk Point at the eastern tip of Long Island, New York.
On August twenty-sixth, eighteen thirty-nine, the United States revenue cutter USS Washington, commanded by Lieutenant Thomas Gedney, spotted the mysterious, ghost-like schooner. Boarding parties seized the Amistad, placing Sengbe and thirty-eight surviving Africans in heavy irons. Gedney, eager to secure a massive maritime salvage award for recovering the valuable ship and its cargo, intentionally steered the captured vessel into the harbor of New London, Connecticut, knowing that slavery was still nominally legal in Connecticut, unlike neighboring New York where the captives would have been instantly set free under state habeas corpus laws.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE NEW HAVEN JAIL AND THE LANGUAGE OF LIBERTY
Transferred to the county jail on the public green in New Haven, Connecticut, the Amistad captives became an overnight international sensation. Crowds of thousands paid admission fees to the jailer to view the exotic 'African pirates' through the iron bars of their cells. Meanwhile, a ferocious diplomatic and legal crisis erupted. The Spanish Crown formally demanded that President Martin Van Buren immediately surrender the ship, cargo, and captives to Spanish authorities in Cuba to face execution for piracy and murder. Van Buren, a vulnerable Democrat facing re-election in eighteen forty and desperate to maintain the political support of Southern slaveholding plantation owners, fully agreed, ordering federal prosecutors to do everything possible to deport the Africans without trial.
Standing against the full weight of the federal government was the newly formed Amistad Committee, led by prominent New York merchant Lewis Tappan and Connecticut abolitionists Simeon Jocelyn and Joshua Leavitt. They hired brilliant local attorneys, including Roger Sherman Baldwin, grandson of Declaration of Independence signer Roger Sherman. But Baldwin faced an insurmountable legal barrier: neither the lawyers nor the courts could communicate with the prisoners, who spoke only Mende and understood not a word of English or Spanish.
In a stroke of investigative brilliance, Yale linguistics professor Josiah Willard Gibbs walked the docks of New York City and Boston for weeks, counting loudly in Mende on his fingers: 'Eta, fili, sia, naani...' Finally, in the port of New York, Gibbs encountered James Covey, a young British sailor who was himself a liberated Mende speaker. Brought to the New Haven jail, Covey began speaking in their native tongue. For the first time, Sengbe Pieh and his comrades were able to tell their harrowing true story to an American court: they were not Spanish slaves, but free African citizens kidnapped in violation of international law.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE DISTRICT COURT TRIUMPH AND VAN BUREN'S TREACHERY
In January eighteen forty, the federal trial convened inside the New Haven courthouse under United States District Judge Andrew T. Judson—a man previously known for his pro-slavery sympathies. Attorney Roger Sherman Baldwin presented overwhelming physical and testimonial evidence proving that the fraudulent Spanish passports were complete fabrications and that the captives were native Africans unlawfully enslaved after the eighteen twenty international treaty.
To the shock and outrage of the Van Buren administration, Judge Judson ruled completely in favor of the Africans, declaring that Sengbe Pieh and his companions were 'born free, and ever since have been, and still of right are, free and not slaves.' He ordered them released from criminal custody and placed under the protection of the federal government to be repatriated back to Africa.
President Van Buren was incandescent with political rage. Refusing to accept the verdict, the president ordered the United States Attorney to appeal the case immediately to the Circuit Court and subsequently to the United States Supreme Court. Van Buren was so determined to pacify Southern politicians that he secretly ordered the navy schooner USS Grampus to anchor in New Haven harbor, with sealed orders instructing the captain to snatch the Africans the moment any court ruled against them and sail them to Havana before their lawyers could file an appeal.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: OLD MAN ELOQUENT BEFORE THE SUPREME COURT
Recognizing that the battle for the Mende captives' lives would face a hostile Supreme Court dominated by five Southern slaveholding justices, including Chief Justice Roger B. Taney, Lewis Tappan traveled to Quincy, Massachusetts, to recruit the most formidable legal orator in America: seventy-three-year-old former President John Quincy Adams.
Nicknamed 'Old Man Eloquent,' Adams had served as ambassador, secretary of state, president, and now represented Massachusetts in the House of Representatives, where he led the fight against the congressional 'gag rule.' Adams had not argued a case before the Supreme Court in thirty-two years and confessed to friends that he trembled with anxiety at his advanced age. Yet when he stood before the Supreme Court in Washington on February twenty-fourth, eighteen forty-one, Adams delivered an eight-and-a-half-hour masterclass in constitutional law, natural rights, and moral outrage that shook the chamber.
Pointing his quivering finger directly at a copy of the Declaration of Independence hanging on the courtroom wall, Adams thundered against the executive overreach of President Van Buren, accusing the president of prostituting the American navy and justice system to act as slave-catchers for a foreign monarchy. Adams proclaimed: 'The moment you come to the declaration that all men are endowed by their Creator with certain inalienable rights, among which are life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, then the case of the Amistad is decided. I ask for nothing more in behalf of these unfortunate men than this court would grant to any citizen of the United States: justice!'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE RETURN TO AFRICA AND THE TORCH OF ABOLITION
On March ninth, eighteen forty-one, Justice Joseph Story delivered the Supreme Court's historic seven-to-one decision. The highest court in the land affirmed that Sengbe Pieh and his companions were free men who had exercised their natural, lawful right of self-defense against unlawful piracy and enslavement. The Supreme Court ordered their immediate, unconditional discharge from all custody.
In New Haven, church bells pealed across the green as the Mende prisoners were formally liberated from jail. For several months, Sengbe and his companions toured New England towns, speaking to packed churches and lecture halls to raise funds for their voyage home. Sengbe spoke with mesmerizing rhetorical power, translated by James Covey, while eleven-year-old Margru and the other children demonstrated their newly learned reading skills.
In November eighteen forty-one, having raised the necessary funds through the Amistad Committee, thirty-five surviving Mende Africans, accompanied by five Christian missionaries, boarded the barque Gentleman in New York harbor. In January eighteen forty-two, after three long years of captivity, trials, and international peril, Sengbe Pieh stepped back onto the soil of Sierra Leone a free man.
The Amistad affair was a monumental watershed in American history. It exposed the moral bankruptcy of the federal government's complicity with slavery and laid the organizational groundwork for the American Missionary Association, which went on to establish hundreds of schools and colleges for freed slaves after the Civil War. In New Haven, a striking fourteen-foot bronze memorial depicting Sengbe Pieh in three relief panels stands on the lawn of City Hall, an eternal monument to the triumph of law, moral conviction, and the unyielding human thirst for liberty.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Amistad rebellion proved that natural rights and moral justice could triumph over legal oppression, inspiring generations of American abolitionists. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we sail into Narragansett Bay for the daring raid on the British schooner HMS Gaspee.
